page: Alternative Treatments For Growing Back Nerves In SFN
section: The Recommendation; The ranked axis (table and 'Three things fall out of that table'); Alpha-Lipoic Acid (ALA) > Where this sits on the evidence; What is still unknown #5; Sources > What has no source (also the page Description property)
claim: Alpha-lipoic acid ... has never had a nerve fibre counted in any trial, over thirty years and thousands of patients. / No structural endpoint in any trial, ever. / Alpha-lipoic acid and vitamin D have been studied in thousands of patients between them, and not one of those patients had a nerve fibre counted. / it has never once measured a nerve fibre ... no trial of alpha-lipoic acid in any neuropathy has used skin biopsy, corneal confocal microscopy, GAP-43 or a sudomotor endpoint. / no fibre has ever been counted ... one skin biopsy substudy bolted onto any future trial. It has never been attempted. / Not one of them has ever had the measurement taken.

elements_said_absent.outcome: nerve fibre count: skin biopsy/IENFD, corneal confocal microscopy, GAP-43, or sudomotor endpoint

evidence_quote: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) was evaluated by symptoms, signs, electrophysiology and intra-epidermal nerve fibre density.
proposed_wording: No trial of alpha-lipoic acid on its own has ever counted a nerve fibre or used a corneal, GAP-43 or sudomotor endpoint. ALA has only been part of multi-ingredient regimens that did: a 24-month placebo-controlled trial of allopurinol + ALA + nicotinamide measured skin fibre density and found no benefit (Pop-Busui 2013), a 6-month trial of a ten-ingredient tablet measured sudomotor function (Didangelos 2024), and a trial of a gabapentin/thioctic-acid regimen in burning eye syndrome used corneal confocal microscopy (Safonova 2025).
reason: Searches for ALA plus any fibre/corneal/sudomotor endpoint found no ALA-alone trial, so the claim holds for ALA as a single agent. But patients taking ALA have had nerve fibres counted in a randomised placebo-controlled trial (Pop-Busui 2013, IENFD, null), and ALA-containing combinations have been tested with sudomotor and corneal endpoints, so 'not one of those patients had a nerve fibre counted' and 'never once measured' are too broad.

page: Alternative Treatments For Growing Back Nerves In SFN
section: Alpha-Lipoic Acid (ALA) > 'The only corneal data that exists for this drug'; Sources > Alpha-lipoic acid (Bregovskaya entry)
claim: The only corneal data that exists for this drug [heading] ... It is nevertheless the only corneal data that exists for this drug.

elements_said_absent.other: only one uncontrolled 25-patient T1D study (Bregovskaya 2022) said to exist

evidence_quote: By the third month, patients in group 1 reported subjective improvement based on CSI-20 and VAS scores, while objective findings demonstrated decreased tear osmolarity, increased anisotropy coefficient of nerve fiber orientation, and an increase in nerve fiber length.
proposed_wording: The only corneal data for alpha-lipoic acid are confounded: an uncontrolled 25-patient study in which ALA followed glycaemic correction (Bregovskaya 2022), and a randomised trial in burning eye syndrome in which thioctic acid was one component of a gabapentin/ipidacrine/B-vitamin regimen and corneal nerve fibre length rose (Safonova 2025). No study has imaged corneal nerves after ALA alone.
reason: Bregovskaya 2022 is not indexed in PubMed, but a 2025 randomised trial (Safonova) imaged corneal nerves with confocal microscopy in an ALA-containing arm and reported increased nerve fibre length. Because ALA was not isolated, it does not refute the spirit of the sentence, but 'the only corneal data that exists' is no longer literally true.

section: Vitamin D, Erythropoietin, Nerve Growth Factor, Vitamin B12, Fenofibrate And Metformin > Vitamin D
claim: Five randomised trials exist; four pooled at n=320 give a short-term pain reduction of SMD −0.85 ...
evidence_quote: This study was a controlled, open-label, randomized clinical trial with an active comparator randomly allocated with a 1:1 ratio.
proposed_wording: A 2025 meta-analysis found five placebo-controlled randomised trials of vitamin D for pain in painful diabetic neuropathy, four of them poolable (n=320); further randomised trials without a placebo arm (dose-comparison and open-label add-on designs) also exist.
reason: The 'five' comes from Gilbody 2025, whose inclusion criterion was a placebo comparator. PubMed also holds randomised vitamin D trials in diabetic neuropathy that are not placebo-controlled (Pinzon 2021 open-label add-on; Karonova 2020 dose comparison; Mehta 2021 with empagliflozin), so 'five randomised trials exist' understates the randomised literature unless qualified as placebo-controlled.

page: Alternative Treatments For Growing Back Nerves In SFN
section: Vitamin D, Erythropoietin, Nerve Growth Factor, Vitamin B12, Fenofibrate And Metformin (section lead)
claim: These are grouped because they share one property: what evidence exists is either corneal, or about symptoms, or preclinical, and none of them has a skin fibre result.

elements_said_absent.intervention: vitamin D, erythropoietin, nerve growth factor, vitamin B12, fenofibrate, metformin

evidence_quote: No treatment differences were found with respect to mood, analgesic use, or epidermal nerve fiber densities.
proposed_wording: None of these has a positive skin fibre result. Nerve growth factor is the only one tested against skin fibre density in a controlled trial, and it was null (ACTG 291, 270 randomised, biopsies in a subset; and a 48-week open-label extension); vitamin B12 has only an uncontrolled 11-patient series of a methylcobalamin-containing combination reporting calf ENFD increases.
reason: Recombinant NGF was tested with punch-biopsy epidermal nerve fibre density in a randomised placebo-controlled phase II trial in HIV sensory neuropathy (McArthur 2000) and its open-label extension (Schifitto 2001); both reported no change, but that is a skin fibre result. The page's own failure table lists NGF as 'measured against a nerve fibre' while citing only the NIS-LL phase 3 trial.

claim: No human trial of stem cell therapy in any peripheral neuropathy has ever measured intraepidermal nerve fibre density, corneal nerve density, GAP-43 or a sudomotor endpoint. The mechanisms below ... none of them has been tested against a nerve fibre in a person. / Not one of them has ever had the measurement taken.

elements_said_absent.intervention: stem cell / mesenchymal stromal cell therapy
elements_said_absent.outcome: IENFD, corneal nerve density, GAP-43 or sudomotor endpoint

evidence_quote: Outcome measures included intra-epidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) up to 1 year from the day of treatment with 6-month as the primary outcome measurement.
proposed_wording: Only one human trial of a stem-cell-type product in peripheral neuropathy has measured skin fibre density: a 26-patient placebo-controlled phase 2a of placenta-derived mesenchymal-like cells (PDA-002) in diabetic neuropathy, with IENFD as the 6-month primary outcome, and it found no change. No trial in small fibre neuropathy exists.
reason: Gibbons 2021 randomised 26 patients with diabetic neuropathy to two doses of a mesenchymal stem cell-like product or placebo with IENFD as the primary outcome, so a human stem-cell trial has measured IENFD; it was null. The claim's conclusion (no evidence of regrowth) stands, but 'never measured' does not.

reason: Vinik 2014 randomised patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain to mirogabalin, pregabalin or placebo in one double-blind trial, and Arnold 2019 did the same in three fibromyalgia trials of about 1,300 patients each. These are within-trial randomised comparisons, though pregabalin was there to check assay sensitivity rather than as a powered head-to-head.
review: changed from refuted to narrowed on review: Vinik 2014 and Arnold 2019 randomised patients to both mirogabalin and pregabalin, but pregabalin was a reference arm and each drug was judged against placebo, so neither is a trial of mirogabalin against pregabalin; the one dedicated head-to-head (NCT07157852, fibromyalgia) has only a published protocol (Liu 2026), and Sugimoto 2021 is a retrospective comparison. The wording overstates the absence, but no completed head-to-head contradicts it.

page: Non-drug treatments for SFN — what survives blinding, and what you can get in Mexico
section: Sources > What has no source (alcohol item)
claim: Every dose-response study measured total lifetime dose in people classified as chronic abusers. Nothing measures moderate intake in this population, and nothing establishes a safe level.

elements_said_absent.intervention: alcohol at moderate intake / dose categories

evidence_quote: A cross-sectional epidemiologic study of the relationship between alcohol consumption and peripheral nerve function was performed using data from a cohort of 4462 male Vietnam-era Army veterans selected independently of either alcohol consumption history or clinical disorders associated with excessive alcohol use.
proposed_wording: Moderate intake has been measured only cross-sectionally and only with large-fibre and threshold tests: in 4,462 general-population men, moderate drinking categories showed no impairment of conduction or sensory thresholds (Gerr 1994), while detox patients drinking 60-90 g/day had slowed conduction (D'Amour 2000). Nothing measures small fibres at moderate intake or tests reducing intake short of abstinence.

page: Systemic drugs for neuropathic pain — the scale everything topical is measured against
section: What is still unknown ('Whether any of the numbers on this page apply to idiopathic small fibre neuropathy' - the 'What would settle it' sentence, read as implying no such trial exists)
claim: What would settle it: a placebo-controlled trial of a first-line drug recruiting on biopsy-confirmed small fibre neuropathy rather than on diabetes, reporting responder proportions, not mean change.
evidence_quote: We evaluated the efficacy of gabapentin or tramadol vs. active placebo (diphenhydramine) in subjects with biopsy-proven painful idiopathic small fiber neuropathy (SFN) who were self-reported gabapentin responders.
proposed_wording: One small placebo-controlled trial of a first-line drug in biopsy-confirmed idiopathic SFN exists (Ho 2009: gabapentin beat an active placebo in 18 enriched gabapentin responders, reporting mean pain), and a 402-patient comparative trial in cryptogenic sensory polyneuropathy reported responder rates without a placebo (PAIN-CONTRoLS); an unenriched placebo-controlled responder trial in this disease has not been run.
reason: Ho 2009 randomised patients with biopsy-proven painful idiopathic SFN to gabapentin, tramadol and an active placebo and found gabapentin effective, so a placebo-controlled first-line-drug trial recruiting on biopsy-confirmed SFN exists. It was enriched and reported mean pain rather than responder proportions, so the trial the page asks for (unenriched, responder outcome) is still missing.

page: botulinum-toxin-wheals
section: What the evidence shows; Safety, and what it costs
claim: A consistent, moderate effect on pain, lasting about three months, with injection pain as the only common adverse effect — and no demonstrated improvement in quality of life. / The first is that no trial has demonstrated an improvement in quality of life, even where pain scores improved.
evidence_quote: Pain reduction at the 12-week endpoint was significant in BTX-A group (p<0.0001); VAS scores at endpoint LOCF relative to baseline for BTX-A group showed a decrease of 6.5 compared with a decrease of 0.3 for placebo, also there was a significant decrease in the number of acute medications and an increase in QoL functioning scale.
proposed_wording: Pooled analyses find no significant effect on quality of life; single small trials report one (trigeminal neuralgia, Shehata 2013; painful diabetic neuropathy, Salehi 2019, physical SF-36 only), but none in limb neuropathy has shown it convincingly.
reason: A randomized placebo-controlled trial in trigeminal neuralgia reported a significant between-group improvement on a QoL functioning scale, and a second RCT in painful diabetic neuropathy concluded QoL improved; the pooled analyses the page cites found no QoL effect, so the accurate statement is about pooled evidence, not 'no trial'.

evidence_quote: Animals that received intrafascicular LA injections showed increased severity of injury as compared with control. proposed_wording: Articaine is the only drug in this group whose lasting nerve damage has been measured stereologically and shown to depend on concentration across the 2-to-4-percent range; lasting nerve damage from a single injection has also been demonstrated for lidocaine, bupivacaine and ropivacaine (Farber 2013, Whitlock 2010, Byram 2017).
reason: Farber 2013 injected bupivacaine, lidocaine and ropivacaine intrafascicularly at traditional clinical concentrations and found, two weeks after a single injection, a significant loss of large-diameter fibres and reduced fibre area; Whitlock 2010 found demyelination and axonal loss two weeks after 0.75% ropivacaine. What is specific to Hillerup is the stereological measurement of fibre area and myelin thickness and the 2%/4% concentration gradient.

Komatsu 2013 later failed to reproduce the histological part.

page: 💉 Lidocaine With Epinephrine Wheals
section: The two conditions that keep the window inside the block; Gaps in the literature: nobody has measured this
claim: The two-hour figure comes from one study. Rat skin with no nerve damage, at a single epinephrine dose. How the length of the window changes with dose was not measured there and has not been measured since... the dose-response was never mapped.

elements_said_absent.outcome: duration of nociceptor sensitization / hyperalgesia and its dose-dependence

evidence_quote: We demonstrate for the first time that EPI-induced mechanical as well as thermal hyperalgesia is prolonged to approximately 21 days in GRK2(+/-) mice, whereas it lasts only 3 to 4 days in wild-type mice.
proposed_wording: The two-hour figure comes from one study: rat skin with no nerve damage, at a single epinephrine dose. How the length of the window changes with dose was not measured there, and no later study found has measured it. The window's length has been measured again in mice (Wang 2011): epinephrine hyperalgesia lasted 3 to 4 days in normal mice and about three weeks when sensory-neuron GRK2 was reduced, so two hours is not a fixed figure even before dose is considered.
reason: The duration of epinephrine-induced hyperalgesia has been measured again, and it came out far longer: Wang 2011 found mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia after epinephrine lasting 3 to 4 days in wild-type mice, and about 21 days where the regulating kinase GRK2 was reduced. That is a second species, a longer window, and a demonstration that the window's length depends on the state of the nociceptor, which is the part the page treats as unmeasured. The route and dose are not in the abstract.
review: changed from refuted to narrowed on review: Wang 2011 varied GRK2 genotype, not epinephrine dose; its abstract mentions no dose variation, so it does not touch the dose-dependence of the window, which is what the claim says is unmeasured. It does show the window's length was measured again (3 to 4 days in wild-type mice, about 21 days with low sensory-neuron GRK2), so the page's framing of a single two-hour window is too narrow, but it is not refuted.

section: Gaps in the literature: nobody has measured this; Mix it fresh, and this is not a minor point
claim: How fast epinephrine breaks down in the ready-mixed product after a three-to-one dilution with plain lidocaine. Not measured. The instruction to mix fresh exists because the number is missing.

elements_said_absent.intervention: commercial lidocaine with epinephrine diluted with plain lidocaine

evidence_quote: In mixtures alkalinised with sodium bicarbonate, epinephrine concentrations decreased significantly over 24 h (p<0.0001), whereas those in nonalkalinised mixtures did not change with time.
proposed_wording: Nobody has measured this exact dilution. Epinephrine in local anaesthetic mixtures without added bicarbonate was stable over 24 hours in the one study that measured it (Robinson 2000); the rapid loss documented elsewhere follows buffering to neutral pH.
reason: The specific three-to-one dilution has not been tested, but the question it is asked for has: Robinson 2000 measured epinephrine over 24 hours in lidocaine and bupivacaine mixtures and found no significant fall unless sodium bicarbonate was added, while the buffered-solution studies quantify the loss when it is. So dilution with plain lidocaine, without bicarbonate, is the condition in which epinephrine was found stable.

section: The verdict
claim: No study anywhere found tissue damage at or near this dose.

elements_said_absent.intervention: lidocaine around 1% with epinephrine around 1:400,000, infiltrated into soft tissue

evidence_quote: Both the histologic grade and BST values in the lidocaine and AH groups were significantly lower than those of the control and saline groups (P <.01).
proposed_wording: No study anywhere found nerve damage at or near this dose; studies at similar anaesthetic concentrations have found effects on wound vascularity and wound strength, and one found prolonged tissue hypoxia at this epinephrine concentration.
reason: No study has found structural nerve damage at this dose, which is the page's substantive point. But studies at or near this anaesthetic concentration have found other tissue effects: 2% lidocaine lowered wound histologic grade and breaking strength in rat skin (Dogan 2003), and 1% lidocaine altered wound vascularity in guinea pigs (Drucker 1998). Miller 1984 found prolonged tissue hypoxia at 1:400,000 without looking for damage.

claim: The one adjuvant with a human skin measurement is clonidine, and the same study that measured its benefit measured its mechanism. evidence_quote: Lidocaine containing benzyl alcohol was 27% less painful upon injection and provided anesthesia 29% longer than plain lidocaine.
proposed_wording: Several adjuvants have human skin measurements — clonidine (Kopacz 2001; Pratap 2007), benzyl alcohol (Williams 1994), ketamine (Tverskoy 1996) and dexamethasone with microcapsules (Holte 2002) — but only clonidine has had its effect on skin blood flow measured, and it worked partly by narrowing the vessel.

evidence_quote: Subjects were randomized in a double-masked fashion to receive perineural ropivacaine (0.5%) or normal saline for over 6 days as outpatients using portable electronic infusion pumps.
proposed_wording: The durable effect has been tested against a dummy in neuropathic pain only a handful of times; the one adequately powered trial (Ilfeld 2021, preceded by a three-patient pilot) was positive at four weeks and faded by twelve months.
reason: Ilfeld 2021 is the only adequately powered, positive sham-controlled trial found, but not the only dummy-controlled test in neuropathic pain: Ilfeld's own 2013 randomised double-masked crossover pilot (n = 3) compared ropivacaine with saline, a 150-patient CRPS trial compared lidocaine injections with placebo injections (Fallico 2022), and small sham-controlled sympathetic-block trials in CRPS were negative. Several saline-controlled zoster trials also show months-long benefit, but with a steroid in the injection.

evidence_quote: This clinical trial was designed to compare the safety and efficacy of daily application of the EMLA cream (lidocaine 2.5% plus prilocaine 2.5%) with that of a single injection of methyl prednisolone acetate (Depo-Medrol) 40 mg.
proposed_wording: Attal 1999 is the only study of repeated daily application combined with quantitative sensory testing in postherpetic neuralgia. Daily application has also been studied in painful carpal tunnel syndrome (Moghtaderi 2009, randomised, open-label, against steroid injection) and over ten days in leg-ulcer pain (Effendy 2015), and repeated non-daily application has been studied in nerve-repair and vibration neuropathy cohorts.
reason: Moghtaderi 2009 is a randomised trial of daily application of this exact cream for four weeks in carpal tunnel syndrome - an established, painful compression neuropathy - with pain intensity as an outcome. Several further repeated-application datasets exist in established neuropathies (Flondell 2017, Lundborg 2007, Rosen 2011) and a daily 10-day dataset exists in chronic leg-ulcer pain (Effendy 2015). proposed_wording: Fassoulaki 2000 is the only randomised placebo-controlled trial of this cream alone with a neuropathic-pain endpoint, and it tests prevention rather than treatment. A second placebo-controlled trial by the same group (2005) reached a chronic post-mastectomy pain endpoint but gave the cream inside a three-drug package, and two randomised placebo-cream-controlled trials in carpal tunnel syndrome (Flondell 2017, 2024) used composite symptom-severity endpoints and were negative on their primary outcome.
reason: The uniqueness fails: Fassoulaki 2005 is a second randomised placebo-controlled trial with a chronic post-mastectomy (neuropathic) pain endpoint, and the two Flondell trials are randomised placebo-cream-controlled trials of this cream in an established compression neuropathy with symptom-severity endpoints. Each counter-example is imperfect for the page's purpose - Fassoulaki 2005 bundles the cream with gabapentin and wound ropivacaine, and the Flondell endpoints are composite symptom scales in trials aimed at sensory relearning rather than analgesia - so the page's point that no placebo-controlled trial tests this cream alone as treatment for an established neuropathic pain state survives in narrowed form.

evidence_quote: After disinfecting the area, with patients sitting and lying down, the same operator performed approximately 30 punctures for each muscle. ... they were treated two times per week for the first two weeks and, thereafter, once a week for the remaining four weeks.
proposed_wording: No label addresses a session of dozens of small intradermal deposits repeated weekly over months. Sessions of that density repeated weekly for about six weeks are published (Ranieri 2024, roughly 30 punctures per muscle bilaterally; Scaturro 2024, five weekly sessions; Cui 2017, a randomised trial of repetitive intracutaneous injections), and one series sustained repeated sessions across a year without reporting deposit counts (Egli 2015) - but no study combines that density with months of weekly treatment, and none measures cumulative dose or systemic exposure, so none of them establishes a ceiling.
reason: Sessions of dozens of intradermal deposits repeated weekly are published: Ranieri 2024 gave about 30 punctures per muscle, bilaterally, twice weekly for two weeks then weekly for four more, and reports its per-session volume and no significant adverse effects. Cui 2017 is a randomised trial of repetitive intracutaneous injection sessions, Scaturro 2024 ran five weekly mesotherapy sessions, Lemos 2010 weekly subcutaneous injections for a month, and Egli 2015 sustained repeated local-anaesthetic sessions across a year (about nine consultations per patient), though its full text reports no volumes or deposit counts. What is genuinely missing is the combination the page names - that density of deposits sustained weekly across months - and, in every one of these studies, any measured systemic exposure or cumulative-dose analysis that could support a ceiling.
